content: Naphazoline is an alpha-adrenergic agonist that is FDA-approved for use as a topical ocular vasoconstrictor. It is commonly used to reduce conjunctival congestion by constricting the blood vessels in the conjunctiva. This effect is believed to result from direct stimulation of alpha-adrenergic receptors in the arterioles of the conjunctiva. The recommended dosage for adults is one or two drops instilled into the conjunctival sac(s) every three to four hours as needed. There is limited information regarding off-label use in both adults and pediatric patients. For pediatric patients, safety and effectiveness have not been established, and there is limited FDA guidance on its use in this population. Naphazoline is contraindicated in individuals with anatomically narrow angles, narrow-angle glaucoma, or hypersensitivity to any component of the preparation. Patients undergoing therapy with monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibitors may experience a severe hypertensive crisis if given a sympathomimetic drug like naphazoline. Use in children, particularly infants, may lead to central nervous system (CNS) depression, coma, and significant reductions in body temperature. This medication is intended for topical ophthalmic use only. Caution is advised in patients with hypertension, cardiovascular abnormalities, hyperglycemia (diabetes), hyperthyroidism, infections, or injuries. Common adverse reactions include mydriasis, increased redness, irritation, discomfort, blurred vision, punctate keratitis, lacrimation, and increased intraocular pressure. Systemic side effects may include dizziness, headache, nausea, sweating, nervousness, drowsiness, weakness, hypertension, cardiac irregularities, and hyperglycemia. There is no established FDA guidance on the use of naphazoline during pregnancy, labor, delivery, or in nursing mothers. It is unknown whether naphazoline is excreted in human milk, so caution should be exercised when administering it to nursing women. Similarly, there is no specific FDA guidance on its use in geriatric patients, specific gender or racial populations, or individuals with renal or hepatic impairment. The safety and efficacy of naphazoline in immunocompromised patients have not been established. Naphazoline belongs to the imidazoline class of sympathomimetic amines. It is a white, odorless crystalline powder with a bitter taste, freely soluble in water and alcohol. The pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics of naphazoline are not well-documented in the drug label. Limited information is available regarding its nonclinical toxicology and clinical studies. The medication should be stored at 20°C to 25°C (68°F to 77°F) in a tightly closed container. To prevent contamination, the dropper tip should not touch any surface, including the eyelids or surrounding areas. If the solution changes color or becomes cloudy, it should not be used. There is no established interaction between alcohol and naphazoline, but patients should consult their doctor regarding the effects of alcohol consumption while using this medication. The brand name for naphazoline is AK-Con®, and there is limited information regarding look-alike drug names in the drug label.
